newsitem.title: JAPAN: Next Japan finance minister faces policy headaches.
newsitem.headline: Next Japan finance minister faces policy headaches.

text.p: Applicants for the post of finance minister in Japan's next government would be well advised to think twice before taking on a portfolio that looks likely to be more of a policy hotseat than a political plum.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was still scrambling on Monday to form a government after an election that left his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) 12 seats short of a majority.
Finance Minister Wataru Kubo's Social Democratic Party has been snubbing LDP offers to join a new ruling coalition and if it stands firm, Kubo is likely to step down, analysts said.

Speculation was as yet muted over possible successors, who might anyway have the job for a mere year or so if Hashimoto is forced to form a minority government. But whoever assumes the post faces a plethora of problems, mishandling of which could damage future political success, analysts said.

"The finance minister post is still powerful and influential and a must if you have aspirations to become prime minister in the future. But it has become a dangerous post," said Takashi Kiuchi, chief economist at the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan (LTCB). "If you fail, you fail miserably."
High on the list of headaches are proposals to trim the power of the finance ministry itself, under fire for its handling of banking system woes and for scandals involving senior officials.

"The next minister is mandated to undertake the task of basically eroding the power of the finance ministry and...it is a very difficult task," said Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at CS First Boston in Tokyo.

The ruling coalition unveiled a plan in September to reform the ministry, including the creation of an independent body to assume the supervisory and regulatory powers through which the ministry has exercised control over the financial industry.
The LDP and others have also proposed that the ministry be deprived of its monopoly over the budget-drafting process and that this function be given to the prime minister's office.
How serious the conservative LDP is about such reforms remains in doubt. "Hashimoto has given no sign of where he stands on this issue," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
Were Hashimoto really keen to achieve ministry reform, LDP Secretary General Koichi Kato -- who has long had tense ties with finance bureaucrats -- might be just the man for the job.
"He (Kato) would be an ideal finance minister if the sole object was to accomplish that (reform), but I'm not sure that this is the decision of the prime minister," Kiuchi said.
Kato's chances for the post are also clouded by allegations, which he has denied, of political funding improprieties.

Other agenda items the new minister will have to address include whether to craft a stimulative supplementary budget for the fiscal year to March 1997, the drafting of next year's budget, tax and pension system reform, and lurking financial system woes highlighted by last week's failure of a finance firm with huge debt liabilities of more than $8.8 billion.

Another ticking policy time-bomb is the massive debt legacy -- almost 28 trillion yen ($247 billion) -- left by the former national railroad when it went private nearly a decade ago. "That will be next year's hot potato," Kiuchi said.
Recent finance ministers faced with equally tough agendas have hardly won rave reviews.

Kubo's predecessor Masayoshi Takemura was dubbed worst finance minister of the year by a British magazine in 1995. His tiny reformist Sakigake Party has dwindled to a mere two seats in the powerful Lower House following the election and earlier defections to the fledgling Democratic Party.
Kubo, meanwhile, looked set to resign as deputy chief of the Social Democrats following their heavy losses in the election, domestic media said. ($1=113 yen)
